n0001.title: Cargo Cult Science
n0001.gist: Research that copies science's outward form while skipping honest self-doubt looks scientific but never actually works.
n0001.question: Cargo cult science — what separates real science from research that only looks like it? (an address with examples)

n0002.title: Masthead
n0002.gist: A short byline and dateline identifying the speech's author and occasion.

n0006.title: A commencement address on self-deception
n0006.gist: Feynman frames his 1974 Caltech speech as a set of remarks on science, pseudoscience, and the discipline of not fooling oneself.
n0006.question: The talk's subject — what is this speech actually about? (a one-line framing)

n0008.title: Belief in a non-scientific world
n0008.gist: A science-saturated age still breeds witch-doctor-style beliefs, so Feynman sets out to investigate why so many people trust things that do not work.
n0008.question: Modern superstition — why do so many people believe things science cannot support? (a survey of examples)

n0009.title: Scientific method and modern superstition
n0009.gist: Science arose from a simple test-and-discard method, yet an otherwise scientific age still cannot explain why witch-doctor-style beliefs ever took hold.

n0013.title: Chasing mysticism and ESP firsthand
n0013.gist: Feynman's own excursions into isolation tanks, Esalen, reflexology, and a failed Uri Geller demonstration show how overwhelming and unverified such popular beliefs are.

n0016.title: Education and crime as witch doctoring
n0016.gist: Widely trusted fields like reading instruction and criminal rehabilitation count as scientific yet show no real progress, resembling the witch doctor's remedy that never works.

n0021.title: Naming Cargo Cult Science
n0021.gist: Feynman names the failures he has surveyed Cargo Cult Science: they copy science's outward form exactly, but something essential is missing, so the planes never land.
n0021.question: Cargo Cult Science — what is this pattern of failure and why does it still not work? (a parable and a diagnosis)

n0025.title: Scientific integrity as leaning over backwards
n0025.gist: Real science demands a deliberate, demanding honesty: reporting every fact and alternative explanation that could undermine your own claim, not just the evidence that supports it.
n0025.question: Scientific integrity — what extra honesty does real science demand beyond ordinary truthfulness? (several illustrations)

n0026.title: Disclosing disconfirming facts
n0026.gist: A theory's advocate must list every fact that disagrees with it as well as those that agree, and must show the theory explains something beyond what it was built to fit.

n0029.title: Honest advertising versus science
n0029.gist: A true statement like 'Wesson Oil doesn't soak through food' can still mislead by implication, and this gap between literal truth and honest implication is what scientific integrity must close.

n0031.title: Why carelessness gets exposed
n0031.gist: Because other experimenters will repeat your work and nature itself will agree or disagree with your theory, only real care not to fool yourself earns a lasting scientific reputation.

n0034.title: The Millikan oil-drop lesson
n0034.gist: Scientists' own history of fooling themselves is shown by the slow, embarrassed drift of electron-charge measurements away from Millikan's slightly wrong original value.
n0034.question: Millikan's electron charge — how did scientists gradually fool themselves about a wrong measurement? (a historical case)

n0038.title: Not fooling yourself or the public
n0038.gist: Because you are the easiest person to fool, scientific integrity starts with self-honesty and extends to never misleading the layman about what your work actually does.
n0038.question: Self-deception and the public — what duty of honesty does a scientist owe first to themselves, then to outsiders? (a principle plus two cases)

n0039.title: The first principle: don't fool yourself
n0039.gist: Feynman states that the first and hardest rule of scientific integrity is not fooling yourself, since after that, honesty toward other scientists follows easily.

n0041.title: Honesty toward the layman
n0041.gist: Scientists owe laypeople the same bending-over-backwards honesty as fellow scientists, illustrated by a colleague who wanted to overstate the practical uses of his own research to keep funding.

n0044.title: Publishing results both ways
n0044.gist: Honest science requires publishing a test's result whichever way it comes out, since selective publication, as with cigarette advertising or politically convenient government advice, is not real scientific advice.

n0047.title: Poor science versus careful science
n0047.gist: Contrasting cases, from psychology students to a national accelerator to a meticulous rat experiment, show the difference between science that controls for every hidden variable and science that does not.
n0047.question: Rigor in practice — what distinguishes experiments that control every variable from those that don't? (case studies)

n0048.title: Skipping the repeat experiment
n0048.gist: A psychology student was told not to replicate a prior rat experiment before varying its conditions, a 1935 policy of changing conditions without ever confirming the original result still held.

n0052.title: Funding pressure in physics
n0052.gist: Even modern physics risks the same shortcut: a researcher compared his new data to someone else's old experiment on different apparatus because funding pressure left no time to redo it properly.

n0054.title: Young's rigorous rat experiment
n0054.gist: Unlike sloppy maze studies, Young systematically eliminated every possible cue, sight, smell, sound, and light, until only true learning let rats find the correct door, a model of real control.

n0059.title: Cargo cult patterns in research today
n0059.gist: Later researchers ignored Young's careful method, and parapsychology experiments keep shrinking toward nothing and refusing the demand for repeatability, both signs of science that has lost its honesty.
n0059.question: Ongoing cargo cult science — where does this failure to be honestly careful persist today? (two cases)

n0063.title: A closing wish for integrity
n0063.gist: Feynman closes by wishing graduates the freedom to keep scientific integrity even under institutional or financial pressure, plus a final practical piece of advice.
n0063.question: Closing wish — what does Feynman hope for the graduates as they leave? (a wish and a piece of advice)
